sentenceSets.sentence: The editor asked for a two-hundred-word précis of the manuscript before she would commit to reading all six hundred pages.

answerChoices.reasoning: A synopsis conventionally traces the story's events in order, but an editor deciding whether to invest in six hundred pages wants the whole work compressed to its essentials rather than a plot walkthrough.
An excerpt would give her two hundred words lifted from one place, which tells her nothing about what the other pages contain.
A blurb is promotional copy written to sell a finished book to buyers, while this is requested privately to inform an editorial decision.
A prologue is part of the manuscript itself and would be one more thing to read rather than a condensation of the whole.
A dedication names the person the book honors and says nothing about its contents.
A manifesto declares a program of intent, whereas the editor wants to learn what the existing manuscript contains.
An epigraph is a quotation set at the head of a work and does not summarize it.
A contract would follow a decision to publish, and she has not yet agreed even to read the book.
A sequel is a further book entirely, not a shorter account of this one.
Amplifying makes a text longer, defeating the purpose of a two-hundred-word request.
The design of letters has nothing to do with what the editor is asking to be written.

sentenceSets.sentence: Every treaty in the archive is filed with a French-language précis prepared by the clerk who first received it.

answerChoices.reasoning: An abstract is normally composed by the document's own author and travels with it from the start, but these were written afterward by the receiving clerk as a finding aid.
A translation renders the treaty's full text into another language, whereas one clerk producing a filing companion for every treaty implies a short condensed account.
A transcription copies the document out at full length, which would double the archive rather than aid searching it.
Annotations are remarks keyed to particular passages, not a single freestanding document filed alongside the treaty.
Ratification is the formal act of approving a treaty, performed by a state rather than by a clerk at intake.
An addendum adds new terms to the agreement itself and could not be the clerk's own work.
A seal authenticates a document but conveys none of its content.
A receipt acknowledges that something arrived without describing what it says.
A forgery is a fraudulent document, which an archive would not routinely file with every treaty as a matter of procedure.
Lengthening each treaty would serve no archival purpose.
A light fixture cannot be filed with a document.

sentenceSets.sentence: He could not write a précis to save his life, returning from every assignment with a summary longer than the article itself.

answerChoices.reasoning: An abridgment shortens a work by cutting passages out of it, but the task he keeps failing is to restate an article's essentials in his own compact account.
A caption labels an image and is not produced by reading an article.
A headline names the story in a phrase, whereas his failure is producing prose that runs longer than the source, which implies the assignment was a condensed account of it.
A critique judges the article's merits, and length would not be the measure of its failure in the way the sentence makes it.
A rebuttal argues against the article, but his assignments involve reporting what it says.
A citation records where a source may be found and could never exceed an article in length.
An interview is conducted with a person, not produced by reading an article.
A footnote supplies a small aside and is not the whole product of an assignment.
A treatise is expected to be long, so producing one would not be a failure.
Collecting many works together is the opposite of the compression he cannot manage.
An object carried against rain is not something one writes.
